executive_assessment.text: Majuro consultations identify access barriers around Ajeltake–Laura, differentiated high-tide support gaps and participant-reported heat/GBV concerns; these are local accounts, not national prevalence.

Leasehold incentives and conditional relocation/resource pressures matter for adaptation design. Community solidarity and communication outputs add capacity, with seawall progress retained at its April 2025 vintage.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2023 reports: In Majuro, inundation disrupts livelihoods and can block Ajeltake-Laura youth from school or town; women, youth and disabled residents reported inadequate high-tide support.
Source dated 2023 reports: Majuro women reported heat-related declines in socializing and increased abuse and gender-based violence.
Source dated 2023 reports: Majuro business participants said leasehold land weakens incentives to invest in flood-proofing buildings that eventually revert to landlords.
Source dated 2023 reports: Participants reported food/water sharing and cleanups; the report identifies solidarity and cooperation as a climate-response asset.
Source dated 2023 reports: Most consulted Majuro participants favored in-place adaptation; 10% of Day-in-Life respondents considered migration after an extreme sea-level briefing.

Source dated 2023-12-05 reports: The report links environmental stress and outer-island food/water insecurity to movement toward crowded Majuro/Ebeye, potentially raising resource competition and discontent.
Source dated 2025-04-15 reports: At the April 2025 mission, the Ebeye seawall contractor was mobilized and works were reported on schedule; protection outcomes were not yet reported.
Source dated 2018-06-22 reports: GFDRR says the assessment analyzed waves, storm surges, typhoons and tsunamis for Majuro and Ebeye, with detailed inundation and erosion risk analysis for Ebeye.

known_gaps.text: No countrywide causal estimate of climate impacts on conflict or violence is established by these sources.
Full subnational coverage and independently evaluated long-term response effectiveness remain gaps.
Local exposure examples do not establish that climate change caused migration or conflict.

The bank contains no completed mediated climate-FCV pathway; this is an evidence gap, not evidence of absence.
The national RMI NAP PDF and 36-page My Heritage Is Here consultation report could not be opened; indexed text from those inaccessible documents was excluded.
The full Ebeye coastal-risk technical report was too large to retrieve; the single claim uses only the official GFDRR landing-page summary.
The accessed community consultation summary covers Majuro only; the assessed northern and southern atoll patterns do not constitute comprehensive subnational coverage.
The direct climate-FCV claims are conditional risks or participant reports; no countrywide causal estimate or observed violence escalation is established.
No reviewed source documents organized conflict blocking a named climate-adaptation intervention; this is an evidence gap, not evidence of absence.
World Bank project outputs and April 2025 seawall progress are historical by the 2026 review date; no later completion/effectiveness report was accessed.

Main directly checked consultation heat/GBV and tenure passages, UNDP conditional relocation/mobility mechanisms, and the historical World Bank ISR. No new observed climate-caused violence is inferred.
